fetched_contents.text: Effects of tunneling on groundwater flow and swelling of clay‐sulfate rocks - Butscher - 2011 - Water Resources Research 1. Introduction [2] Tunneling in clay-sulfate rocks often faces substantial engineering problems because of the swelling behavior of such rock [Einstein, 1996; Anagnostou et al., 2010]. The swelling manifests itself by heave of the tunnel floor, destruction of the lining, or even uplift of the entire tunnel and the ground surface above [e.g., Anagnostou, 1992]. Rehabilitation of damaged tunnels causes disruption of major transportation links and produces high additional costs. Examples of tunnels that are affected by swelling clay-sulfate rocks include tunnels crossing the Triassic Gipskeuper (“gypsum Keuper,” GK) formation in the Jura Mountains of Switzerland and France, and in the Stuttgart metropolitan area in Germany [Steiner, 1993]. Engineering problems related to the swelling of clay-sulfate rocks are also reported from other countries, including Spain [Alonso and Olivella, 2008], Saudi Arabia [Azam, 2007], Poland, Italy, and Texas [Yilmaz, 2001, and references therein]. It is likely, although not known by the authors, that more cases exist elsewhere. The problems associated with the swelling are likely to gain even more relevance in the near future. In the area of Stuttgart, for example, a major railway project (Stuttgart 21 [Wittke, 2007]) is currently planned that involves many additional kilometers of underground infrastructure within the Gipskeuper. [3] The threat of swelling is mostly counteracted on an engineering level by constructive measures. Countermeasures are planned based on the relation between swelling deformation and swelling pressure. In pure clay rocks, for example, there is a linear relation between swelling heave and the logarithm of pressure [Madsen and Vonmoos, 1989]. In clay rocks containing sulfate minerals, however, an accepted relation describing the heave as a function of pressure is still lacking. In practice, engineers face the problem that swelling heave and pressure are hardly predictable during project planning. Field and laboratory experiments often give contradictory indications [Nüesch et al., 1995], and thermodynamic calculations of crystallization pressures [Ping and Beaudoin, 1992] are not supported by experimental data [Flückiger et al., 1994]. Major problems in swelling experiments arise from the fact that such experiments last extremely long [Pimentel, 2007a, 2007b]. Some of them have been run for more than 20 years without reaching final (equilibrium) conditions. In addition, field-scale conditions controlling the swelling process (actual permeabilities, pore water pressures, geochemistry) are rarely known accurately, and therefore difficult to represent in the laboratory. [4] The basic mechanism that causes the swelling of clay-sulfate rocks is the transformation of the water-free calcium-sulfate anhydrite (CaSO4) into its water-containing modification gypsum (CaSO4 × 2H2O) [e.g., Blount and Dickson, 1973]. This reaction entails an ∼60% volume increase of the transformed sulfate minerals. In a closed system (without water inflow), the volume of gypsum is ∼10% less than that of its educts anhydrite plus water, and an increase in total rock volume cannot be expected. In a system open to water inflow, however, the total rock volume increases when anhydrite transforms into gypsum, provided that the increase in the volume of the sulfate minerals is not compensated by a decrease in pore water volume. Changes in pore water volumes can occur by anhydrite solution and gypsum precipitation during the swelling process. However, the differences in the pore water volume of clay rocks containing anhydrite and clay rocks containing gypsum are considered to be minor, and small changes in pore water volume lead to even smaller changes in total rock volume. From this consideration it follows that observed swelling of clay-sulfate rocks (i.e., an increase in total rock volume) requires both water uptake by anhydrite to form gypsum, and, concurrently, water inflow. Figure 1 shows a volume balance of the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum for clay-sulfate rocks in an open system, assuming a constant pore water volume. [5] Given that water inflow into clay-sulfate rocks is a prerequisite for swelling, groundwater flow is likely to be a major controlling factor of the swelling process. Despite its importance, hydrogeological aspects have attracted little attention in the investigation of swelling processes so far [Hauber et al., 2005]. Butscher et al. [2011a] investigated the effects of regional groundwater flow on swelling clay-sulfate rock in tunneling. They concluded that tunnel excavation causes an increase of flow rates around the tunnel and changes the capture zone and geochemical conditions in the tunnel. They also presented a case study that investigated the hydraulic changes induced by tunneling in the Chienberg tunnel (Switzerland), and related these changes to the swelling in different zones of the tunnel [Butscher et al., 2011b]. The findings suggest that in certain situations the tunnel and its surrounding excavation-damaged zone provide pathways for groundwater flow from water-containing units above the tunnel to anhydritic layers at the tunnel invert. The resulting groundwater inflow into anhydritic layers probably triggers the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum and, thus causes rock swelling. [6] So far, there are two major limitations in the studies that investigated the influence of groundwater flow on the swelling of clay-sulfate rocks. The first concerns model uncertainties in the case studies. Typically, hydraulic properties of the geological units, the tunnel liner, and its surrounding excavation-damaged zone are not well known in tunneling projects. fetched_contents.text: Assessing the impact of tunnelling on karst groundwater balance by using lumped parameter models Introduction Karstic aquifers are characteristic of complex flow geometry and strong hydrogeological heterogeneity, caused mainly by double or triple porosity structures consisting of pores, fissures, fractures and conduits of various scales (White, 2002, Ford and Williams, 2007, Hartmann et al., 2014). Consequently, karst groundwater typically consists of base flow through fissure network and rapid flow through enlarged fractures and conduits (Jukić and Denić-Jukić, 2009, Hosseini et al., 2017). These characteristics give rise to significant challenges in groundwater flow modelling in karstic formations. Further complexity arises when anthropogenic activities, e.g., tunnel construction, are involved, where the groundwater flow paths and discharges may be changed drastically within a short period (Hao et al., 2016, Lv et al., 2020), even resulting in geological and environmental hazards such as mud and water inrush, spring depletion, and ground subsidence (Raposo et al., 2010, Pu et al., 2011, Mahler and Bourgeai, 2013, Grimmeisen et al., 2016, Han et al., 2017, Jiang et al., 2018, Liu et al., 2019, Chen et al., 2020, Zhou et al., 2021). A variety of hydrological models (e.g., black-box, distributed, and lumped) have been proposed to confront the challenges and approximate the groundwater budget changes in karst formations (Beven, 1989, Fleury et al., 2007, Le Moine et al., 2008, Makropoulos et al., 2008, Jukić and Denić-Jukić, 2009, Hartmann et al., 2012). The black-box models treat an aquifer as a black-box system and focus on establishing an overall relationship between input (infiltration) and output (discharge), completely disregarding the structure and the physical mechanisms of the aquifer (Dreiss, 1983, Mangin, 1984). The distributed models solve flow equations with temporal and spatial discretization over the whole aquifer, hence requiring detailed information on the aquifer structure and hydrological properties for producing an acceptable simulation (Zhang et al., 2011, Zheng et al., 2020, Saller et al., 2013). The lumped models provide a compromised tool for karst groundwater simulation in which linear or nonlinear reservoirs/compartments are used to represent different physical elements of the aquifer structure and groundwater circulation (Fleury et al., 2007, Fleury et al., 2009, Jukić and Denić-Jukić, 2009). Each reservoir relies on a production function and a transfer function to simulate the process from input to output in each hydrogeological unit, and hence the lumped models are suitable for aquifer simulation with limited observation data and insufficient field characterization. Spring discharge observations and trace element data are commonly used to calibrate the lumped models (Wagener et al., 2003, Hartmann et al., 2013, Ye et al., 2014, Mudarra et al., 2019). Particular concerns have been focused on the temporal variability in groundwater recharges and the effect of karst aquifers drainage induced by climate change or human activities (Jukić and Denić-Jukić, 2009, Chang et al., 2017, Hosseini et al., 2017). The construction of deep-buried tunnels in karst regions can profoundly change the water budget in the karst system. Hence there is a need to revisit the structure and parameters of the lumped model, for incorporating this strong impact of human activity. This study is motivated by tunnel excavation-induced karst groundwater budget changes in the Jiayan Water Diversion Project (JWDP), located in Guizhou Province, Southwest China. In this work, a modified lumped model is presented to quantitatively estimate the impact of tunnel construction on the karst aquifers, by integrating a channel drainage compartment that represents the drainage from the karst aquifer to the tunnel during construction. The model structure is systematically investigated through comparison of simulations with varying levels of simplification by merging or removing some of the flow components. The dominant hydrogeological processes that control the aquifer discharge are identified by performance assessment of the models and sensitivity analysis of the input parameters. The impact of tunnel construction on the aquifer discharge is finally quantified with the calibrated models, which contributes to decision-making for appropriate engineering treatments during tunnel construction. fetched_contents.text: Reactive Transport Modeling of Swelling Processes in Clay‐sulfate Rocks - Schweizer - 2018 - Water Resources Research 1 Introduction Understanding the hydro-mechanical-chemical processes associated with rock swelling plays an important role for mitigating and preventing the failure of many geotechnical applications. For example, the swelling of argillaceous rock through hydration and osmosis is a decisive factor in selecting geologic formations suitable for hosting rock nuclear waste storage facilities (e.g., Nuclear Decommissioning Authority, 2010) and in determining the stability of well drillings in shales (Fjar et al., 2008). Rock swelling is particularly pronounced in clay-sulfate rocks, such as those found in the Triassic Gypsum Keuper formation in southern Germany. The most severe problems with swelling clay-sulfate rocks are typically encountered during the construction of tunnels, and more recently also in conjunction with vertical ground source heat pump systems (Fleuchaus & Blum, 2017; Grimm et al., 2014). Clay-sulfate rocks may swell substantially upon contact with water, thus creating pressures that can severely damage infrastructure through the heaving of tunnel sections and the ground surface (Anagnostou et al., 2010; Ruch & Wirsing, 2013). Although it is generally accepted that rock swelling is triggered by inflow of water stemming from engineering activities, the processes underlying the actual swelling of clay-sulfate rocks are not yet sufficiently well understood (Butscher, Breuer et al., 2016; Butscher, Mutschler et al., 2016). In particular, the link between hydrogeological and geochemical processes and their resulting response on geomechanical swelling requires further investigation in order to develop effective countermeasures to mitigate or even prevent swelling. This is especially true in settings where the swelling cannot be contained via engineering solutions (Kovári & Chiaverio, 2007; Pierau & Kiehl, 1996). Clay-sulfate rocks consist of a clay matrix that contains finely dispersed anhydrite crystals or anhydrite layers and nodules of varying dimensions, with the actual texture of the rock depending on its pressure and temperature history (e.g., Rauh & Thuro, 2007). In general, clay-sulfate swelling involves two partially superimposed processes: (1) The swelling of clay minerals through osmotic water uptake and hydration (Madsen & Müller-Vonmoos, 1989), and (2) the swelling of sulfates caused by the chemical transformation of anhydrite (CaSO4) into gypsum (CaSO4·H2O) upon contact with water (CaSO4+2H2O↔CaSO4·H2O). The latter process results in a volume increase of up to 61% and is considered to be the main mechanism of swelling in clay-sulfate rocks. The swelling potential, however, is strongly dependent on the specific surface area of the anhydrite crystals and thus on the grain morphology. Finely dispersed anhydrite crystals are particularly prone to swelling due to their relatively large surface area in potential contact with water. Beds of massive anhydrite, in contrast, show relatively little swelling (Rauh & Thuro, 2007). Furthermore, Madsen and Nuesch (1991) showed that the swelling potential of clay-sulfate rocks also depends on the clay content and reaches its maximum at about 15% clay. There are numerous conflicting hypotheses for this causal link and the role of clay in clay-sulfate swelling (see Butscher, Mutschler et al., 2016, for an overview). They range from an increase in water availability for anhydrite through flow paths created by rock disintegration or locally increased permeability, to an influence on the sulfate concentration and thus the anhydrite saturation state, all triggered by the swelling of clay. Expansive clay minerals such as corrensite also appear to play an important, yet not clearly defined, role in the swelling. Possibly they facilitate the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum (Anagnostou et al., 2010; Lippmann, 1976; Wittke, 2014). The mineralogical transformation of anhydrite into gypsum takes place indirectly via the solution phase, with anhydrite dissolving into the pore water and gypsum subsequently precipitating from the solution. Dissolution and precipitation equilibria are controlled by the pore water composition, temperature, and pressure (Serafeimidis & Anagnostou, 2014a, 2014b). Reaction kinetics additionally depend on the available reactive mineral surfaces (Hardie, 1967; Hill, 1937; Serafeimidis & Anagnostou, 2012a). Furthermore, the reaction kinetics depend on the hydrodynamic conditions of the system (Jeschke et al., 2001), which may drastically change during swelling, for example, because the hydraulic properties of discontinuities are altered by gypsum crystallization (Alonso, 2012; Wittke, 2014). Hydrodynamic conditions are also altered by engineering activities, on both the regional and local scales (e.g., Butscher, Einstein et al., 2011; Scheidler et al., 2017), therefore affecting solute transport and water accessibility within the clay-sulfate rocks. Thus, in order to gain a comprehensive understanding of the swelling phenomena, knowledge of the controlling hydrogeological and geochemical conditions and processes, and how these are affected by engineering activities (e.g., geothermal drillings), is of paramount importance. Previous studies have provided important insights into the geochemical processes affecting the CaSO4−H2O system, for example; by determining stability fields of anhydrite and gypsum under various pressure, temperature, and concentration conditions (e.g., Blount & Dickson, 1973; Dai et al., 2017; Freyer & Voigt, 2003; MacDonald, 1953; Marsal, 1952; Partridge & White, 1929), which can be used to characterize the critical conditions that may lead to sulfate dissolution or precipitation. Tunnel excavation alters groundwater flow and stress through a combination of direct hydraulic disruption and indirect stress-relief effects. The evidence shows that excavation-induced groundwater level drawdown is a central issue: during tunneling, groundwater flows into the tunnel, and the water level falls, causing a decrease in the surface water level [N1-R3]. This indicates that excavation creates new flow paths and pressure changes by removing the overlying load and allowing water to move into the excavation zone [N1-F1]. The excavation-damaged zone around the tunnel can become a pathway for groundwater flow, changing the capture zone and geochemical conditions in the tunnel [N1-F1].

Excavation also changes the hydraulic head and pore-pressure field around the tunnel. The hydraulic heads on a slope reflect the steady-state or transient groundwater flow system, and excavation-induced changes can alter those heads [N1-R4]. This means that excavation does not just remove rock; it redistributes water and pressure across the surrounding ground, which is especially important in fractured rock and aquifers where flow paths are already complex [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The cited karst groundwater study emphasizes that tunnel construction can drastically change groundwater flow paths and discharges within a short period, altering the aquifer’s budget and potentially causing mud and water inrush, spring depletion, and ground subsidence [N2-F2]. This supports the idea that excavation creates new flow paths and pressure changes by modifying the connectivity of the subsurface system [N2-R1][N2-F2].

Stress relief from excavation affects permeability and water movement through the mechanical response of the rock mass. The excavation-damaged zone becomes more permeable as stress is relieved, because fractures and discontinuities can open or become more connected [N6-R1]. This increased permeability allows water to flow laterally, triggering chemical transformation and altering hydrodynamic conditions [N6-R1]. The evidence also notes that hydrodynamic conditions are altered by engineering activities on both regional and local scales, which affects solute transport and water accessibility within clay-sulfate rocks [N4-F3]. In the excavation context, this means that stress relief can make the rock mass more vulnerable to water ingress, while the resulting permeability change can either increase or localize flow depending on how the stress field is disturbed [N6-R1][N4-F3].

The zones most vulnerable to flow redistribution are the excavation-damaged zone around the tunnel and the anhydritic layers at the tunnel invert [N1-F1]. The excavation-damaged zone is where the disturbance is most direct and where the tunnel and surrounding rock can act as a conduit for groundwater flow [N1-F1]. The tunnel invert is particularly important because the study explicitly links anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation to water inflow into anhydritic layers, and that process is thought to drive swelling [N1-F1]. These zones are therefore the most exposed to both flow change and subsequent geochemical reaction, making them the most vulnerable to redistribution effects [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Groundwater interacts with clay-sulfate rocks to induce swelling through hydration and mineral reactions that change rock volume. The evidence states that clay-sulfate swelling involves two partially superimposed processes: (1) swelling of clay minerals through osmotic water uptake and hydration, and (2) swelling of sulfates caused by the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum upon contact with water [N4-F3]. This is a key mechanism because it explains how water, not just mechanical stress, can cause expansion [N4-F3].

Water chemistry and saturation levels are important triggers for expansion. The evidence indicates that the conditions controlling dissolution and precipitation of sulfate minerals strongly depend on the geochemistry of the pore water [N4-R2]. In particular, the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum is governed by the pore-water composition, temperature, and pressure [N4-F3]. This means that saturation with water is necessary for swelling, but the exact chemistry of the pore water determines whether dissolution or precipitation dominates and whether the reaction proceeds under conditions favorable to gypsum formation [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that the swelling potential is strongly dependent on the specific surface area of the anhydrite crystals, so finely dispersed anhydrite is particularly prone to swelling [N4-F3]. This shows that not all clay-sulfate rocks respond equally; mineralogy and surface area matter.

Hydration and mineral reactions change rock volume through a combination of clay swelling and anhydrite-to-gypsum transformation. The evidence states that the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum results in a volume increase of up to 61% [N4-F3]. In a closed system, the volume of gypsum is about 10% less than that of its reactants, so a net volume increase only occurs if the sulfate mineral expansion is not compensated by a decrease in pore water volume [N1-F1]. In an open system, water inflow is required for swelling to occur because the water uptake by anhydrite to form gypsum must be accompanied by concurrent water inflow [N1-F1]. This means that groundwater is not only a trigger; it is a necessary medium for the swelling reaction to proceed and for the rock to expand [N1-F1][N4-F3].

The most-prone clay-sulfate minerals are anhydrite and gypsum-bearing clay-sulfate rocks, with anhydrite being especially significant because its hydration into gypsum is the main mechanism of swelling [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that expansive clay minerals such as corrensite may play an important, though not clearly defined, role [N4-F3]. In addition, finely dispersed anhydrite crystals are particularly prone to swelling due to their relatively large surface area in potential contact with water [N4-F3]. So the most-prone zones are those with high anhydrite content, high surface area, and favorable pore-water chemistry [N4-F3]. Clay minerals themselves contribute by enabling water access through osmosis and hydration [N3-R3].

Geochemical conditions control clay-sulfate swelling through pore-water chemistry and solubility thresholds. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that the conditions controlling dissolution and precipitation of sulfate minerals depend strongly on the geochemistry of the pore water [N4-R2]. In particular, the mineralogical transformation of anhydrite into gypsum takes place indirectly via the solution phase, with anhydrite dissolving into the pore water and gypsum subsequently precipitating from the solution [N4-F3]. This shows that swelling is not just a mechanical response; it is a geochemical reaction that depends on whether the pore water is undersaturated or oversaturated relative to gypsum [N4-F3].

Pore-water chemistry and solubility thresholds drive expansion by determining whether anhydrite dissolves or gypsum precipitates. The evidence states that dissolution and precipitation equilibria are controlled by pore-water composition, temperature, and pressure [N4-F3]. It also notes that under low-pressure and low-temperature conditions, which are relevant to Gypsum Keuper formations and tunneling, anhydrite solubility is higher than that of gypsum under certain conditions [N4-F3]. This implies that the geochemical threshold is critical: if the pore water promotes anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation, swelling will occur; if not, the reaction will be suppressed or reversed [N4-F3]. The evidence further states that the swelling potential is strongly dependent on the specific surface area of the anhydrite crystals, so finely dispersed anhydrite is particularly prone to swelling [N4-F3]. This means that the same rock type may behave differently depending on its mineralogy and pore-water chemistry [N4-R2][N4-F3].

Dissolution/precipitation reactions alter effective stress because they change the pore-water volume and the hydraulic properties of the rock mass. The evidence explains that changes in pore water volumes can occur by anhydrite solution and gypsum precipitation during the swelling process [N1-F1]. It also states that hydrodynamic conditions are altered by engineering activities and that reaction kinetics depend on the available reactive mineral surfaces and hydrodynamic conditions [N4-F3]. In the excavation context, this means that swelling can feedback into the stress state by changing the rock’s hydraulic properties and effective stress [N4-F3]. The evidence further notes that the hydraulic properties of discontinuities can be altered by gypsum crystallization, which can change local permeability and flow behavior [N4-F3]. Thus, geochemical reactions do not just cause volume expansion; they can also modify the mechanical response of the rock and the surrounding ground [N4-F3].

Useful geochemical indicators for predicting swelling include pore-water composition, temperature, pressure, anhydrite saturation state, and the presence of expansive clay minerals [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence also implies that the mineralogical transformation of anhydrite into gypsum can be used as an indicator, because the reaction is the main mechanism of swelling in clay-sulfate rocks [N4-F3]. In addition, the study notes that the geochemical processes affecting the CaSO4−H2O system can be characterized by stability fields of anhydrite and gypsum under various conditions, which can help identify critical conditions leading to sulfate dissolution or precipitation [N4-F3]. Therefore, geochemical indicators are most useful when they can be tied to solubility thresholds and the actual pore-water conditions in the rock [N4-R2][N4-F3].

The coupled excavation-groundwater-swelling pathway is built on a feedback loop in which tunnel excavation changes groundwater flow, which in turn creates conditions favorable for swelling, which then alters the rock mass and can amplify further flow redistribution. The upstream evidence shows that excavation creates new flow paths and pressure changes by removing the overlying load and allowing water to move into the excavation zone [N1-R3][N1-F1]. It also changes the hydraulic head and pore-pressure field around the tunnel, altering the groundwater flow system and potentially changing capture zones and geochemical conditions [N1-R4][N1-F1]. Excavation-induced changes can drastically alter groundwater flow paths and discharges in fractured rock and aquifers, sometimes within a short period, and can change the aquifer’s budget and create hazards such as mud and water inrush, spring depletion, and ground subsidence [N2-F2]. Stress relief from excavation can increase permeability by opening fractures and discontinuities, which then facilitates lateral flow and chemical transformation [N6-R1]. These effects combine to make the excavation-damaged zone and the tunnel invert especially vulnerable to flow redistribution [N1-F1].

Excavation-induced flow change can accelerate swelling because it increases water access to clay-sulfate rocks and may favor anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation. The evidence states that tunnel excavation causes an increase in flow rates around the tunnel and changes the capture zone of the tunnel and geochemical conditions [N5-R4]. It also notes that tunnel excavation can create pathways for groundwater flow from water-containing units above the tunnel to anhydritic layers at the tunnel invert, and that the resulting groundwater inflow into anhydritic layers probably triggers the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum and thus causes rock swelling [N1-F1]. This is the key acceleration mechanism: excavation moves water into the rock mass, which then triggers the geochemical reaction that expands the rock [N1-F1][N5-R4].

The feedback loops between water ingress and rock expansion are central. Water entering the rock mass increases saturation and pore-water chemistry, which promotes anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence explains that dissolution and precipitation equilibria are controlled by pore-water composition, temperature, and pressure, and that reaction kinetics depend on available reactive mineral surfaces and hydrodynamic conditions [N4-F3]. In turn, the swelling reaction alters pore-water volume and hydraulic properties, which can change the stress state and effective stress in the rock mass [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The evidence further notes that gypsum crystallization can alter the hydraulic properties of discontinuities, changing local permeability and flow behavior [N4-F3]. So the loop is not just mechanical: water ingress → geochemical reaction → rock expansion → altered stress and permeability → more localized or redirected flow [N1-F1][N4-F3][N6-R1].

The most relevant failure modes in tunneling are tunnel heave, destruction of the tunnel lining, uplift of the entire tunnel and the ground surface above, and the associated engineering disruption and high additional costs [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that swelling problems are especially serious in tunneling because the same mechanisms that cause heave can destroy the tunnel lining and threaten the surface above the tunnel [N1-F1]. In addition, the upstream geochemical evidence indicates that finely dispersed anhydrite crystals are particularly prone to swelling, and that expansive clay minerals such as corrensite may also play an important role [N4-F3]. This means that the failure modes are not just structural; they are also geochemical, and the most vulnerable zones are those where anhydrite is present, permeability has increased, and pore-water chemistry favors gypsum precipitation [N4-F3][N1-F1].

Overall, the pathway is: tunnel excavation → altered groundwater flow and stress → increased water access and permeability → geochemical reaction (anhydrite dissolution/gypsum precipitation) → rock expansion and swelling → feedback on flow and stress → potential failure modes such as heave, lining damage, and surface uplift [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3][N6-R1]. The risks are therefore most acute where excavation-induced flow changes intersect with favorable geochemical conditions in clay-sulfate rocks [N5-R4][N1-F1].

Pore-water chemistry and solubility thresholds drive expansion by determining whether anhydrite dissolves or gypsum precipitates. The evidence states that dissolution and precipitation equilibria are controlled by pore-water composition, temperature, and pressure [N4-F3]. It also notes that under low-pressure and low-temperature conditions, which are relevant to Gypsum Keuper formations and tunneling, anhydrite solubility is higher than that of gypsum under certain conditions [N4-F3]. This implies that the geochemical threshold is critical: if the pore water promotes anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation, swelling will occur; if not, the reaction will be suppressed or reversed [N4-F3]. ## Coupled excavation-groundwater-swelling pathway and risks

The coupled excavation-groundwater-swelling pathway is built on a feedback loop in which tunnel excavation changes groundwater flow, which in turn creates conditions favorable for swelling, which then alters the rock mass and can amplify further flow redistribution. The evidence shows that excavation-induced flow change can accelerate swelling because it increases water access to clay-sulfate rocks and may favor anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation [N5-R4][N1-F1]. The feedback loops between water ingress and rock expansion are central. Water entering the rock mass increases saturation and pore-water chemistry, which promotes anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation [N4-R2][N4-F3]. Putting the evidence together, tunnel excavation affects groundwater flow and leads to swelling in clay-sulfate rocks through a three-part mechanism:

1. **Excavation changes groundwater flow and stress** by creating new flow paths, lowering hydraulic heads, and altering permeability through stress relief [N1-R3][N1-F1][N6-R1].
2. **Groundwater interacts with clay-sulfate rocks to induce swelling** through hydration and mineral reactions, especially the hydration of anhydrite into gypsum, which can increase rock volume by up to 61% [N4-F3].
3. **Geochemical conditions control whether the swelling reaction proceeds** by determining pore-water chemistry, solubility thresholds, and the effective stress state [N4-R2][N4-F3].

The result is a coupled feedback pathway: excavation-induced flow change → increased water access and permeability → geochemical reaction (anhydrite dissolution/gypsum precipitation) → rock expansion and swelling → feedback on flow and stress → potential failure modes such as heave, lining damage, and surface uplift [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3][N6-R1]. This increased permeability allows water to flow laterally, triggering chemical transformation and altering hydrodynamic conditions [N6-R1]. In the excavation context, this means that stress relief can make the rock mass more vulnerable to water ingress, while the resulting permeability change can either increase or localize flow depending on how the stress field is disturbed [N6-R1][N4-F3].

The excavation-damaged zone is where the disturbance is most direct and where the tunnel and surrounding rock can act as a conduit for groundwater flow [N1-F1]. The tunnel invert is particularly important because the study explicitly links anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation to water inflow into anhydritic layers, and that process is thought to drive swelling [N1-F1]. These zones are therefore the most exposed to both flow change and subsequent geochemical reaction, making them the most vulnerable to redistribution effects [N1-F1][N4-F3].

This means that saturation with water is necessary for swelling, but the exact chemistry of the pore water determines whether dissolution or precipitation dominates and whether the reaction proceeds under conditions favorable to gypsum formation [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that the swelling potential is strongly dependent on the specific surface area of the anhydrite crystals, so finely dispersed anhydrite is particularly prone to swelling [N4-F3]. This shows that not all clay-sulfate rocks respond equally; mineralogy and surface area matter.

Hydration and mineral reactions change rock volume through a combination of clay swelling and anhydrite-to-gypsum transformation. The evidence states that the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum results in a volume increase of up to 61% [N4-F3]. In an open system, water inflow is required for swelling to occur because the water uptake by anhydrite to form gypsum must be accompanied by concurrent water inflow [N1-F1]. This means that groundwater is not only a trigger; it is a necessary medium for the swelling reaction to proceed and for the rock to expand [N1-F1][N4-F3].

The most-prone clay-sulfate minerals are anhydrite and gypsum-bearing clay-sulfate rocks, with anhydrite being especially significant because its hydration into gypsum is the main mechanism of swelling [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that expansive clay minerals such as corrensite may play an important, though not clearly defined, role [N4-F3]. In addition, finely dispersed anhydrite crystals are particularly prone to swelling due to their relatively large surface area in potential contact with water [N4-F3]. So the most-prone zones are those with high anhydrite content, high surface area, and favorable pore-water chemistry [N4-F3]. Clay minerals themselves contribute by enabling water access through osmosis and hydration [N3-R3].

## Integrated explanation of how tunnel excavation affects groundwater flow and leads to swelling in clay-sulfate rocks

Tunnel excavation affects groundwater flow and leads to swelling in clay-sulfate rocks through a coupled hydro-mechanical-chemical process. The evidence shows that excavation creates new flow paths and pressure changes by removing the overlying load and allowing water to move into the excavation zone [N1-R3][N1-F1]. At the same time, stress relief from excavation changes permeability and water movement by opening fractures and discontinuities, which can facilitate lateral flow and chemical transformation [N6-R1]. These effects combine to alter the groundwater flow system, change the hydraulic head and pore-pressure field, and modify capture zones and geochemical conditions around the tunnel [N1-R4][N1-F1]. In fractured rock and aquifers, excavation can drastically change groundwater flow paths and discharges, sometimes within a short period, and can alter the aquifer’s budget and create hazards such as mud and water inrush, spring depletion, and ground subsidence [N2-F2]. This establishes the core pathway: excavation-induced disturbance → flow redistribution → stress change → more permeable rock mass.

## How tunnel excavation alters groundwater flow and stress

Excavation creates new flow paths and pressure changes because it disrupts the original subsurface hydraulic system. Groundwater flows into the tunnel during excavation, and the water level falls, causing a decrease in the surface water level [N1-R3]. This means excavation does not simply remove rock; it actively redistributes water and pressure across the surrounding ground [N1-F1]. The hydraulic heads on a slope reflect the steady-state or transient groundwater flow system, and excavation-induced changes can alter those heads [N1-R4]. In practice, tunnel excavation can increase flow rates around the tunnel and change the capture zone of the tunnel and geochemical conditions [N5-R4]. The evidence also notes that tunnel excavation can create pathways for groundwater flow from water-containing units above the tunnel to anhydritic layers at the tunnel invert, which is a key mechanism for redirecting flow into zones where swelling is likely to occur [N1-F1].

Stress relief from excavation affects permeability and water movement by altering the rock mass’s mechanical response. The excavation-damaged zone becomes more permeable as stress is relieved, because fractures and discontinuities can open or become more connected [N6-R1]. This increased permeability allows water to flow laterally, triggering chemical transformation and altering hydrodynamic conditions [N6-R1]. The evidence also states that hydrodynamic conditions are altered by engineering activities on both regional and local scales, which affects solute transport and water accessibility within clay-sulfate rocks [N4-F3]. In the excavation context, this means that stress relief can make the rock mass more vulnerable to water ingress, while the resulting permeability change can either increase or localize flow depending on how the stress field is disturbed [N6-R1][N4-F3].

The zones most vulnerable to flow redistribution are the excavation-damaged zone around the tunnel and the anhydritic layers at the tunnel invert [N1-F1]. The excavation-damaged zone is where the disturbance is most direct, and the tunnel and surrounding rock can act as a conduit for groundwater flow [N1-F1]. The tunnel invert is particularly important because the study explicitly links anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation to water inflow into anhydritic layers, and that process is thought to drive swelling [N1-F1]. These zones are therefore the most exposed to both flow change and subsequent geochemical reaction, making them the most vulnerable to redistribution effects [N1-F1][N4-F3].

## How groundwater interacts with clay-sulfate rocks to induce swelling

Groundwater interacts with clay-sulfate rocks to induce swelling through hydration and mineral reactions that change rock volume. The evidence states that clay-sulfate swelling involves two partially superimposed processes: (1) swelling of clay minerals through osmotic water uptake and hydration, and (2) swelling of sulfates caused by the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum upon contact with water [N4-F3]. This is a key mechanism because it explains how water, not just mechanical stress, can cause expansion [N4-F3].

Water chemistry and saturation levels are important triggers for expansion. The evidence indicates that the conditions controlling dissolution and precipitation of sulfate minerals strongly depend on the geochemistry of the pore water [N4-R2]. In particular, the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum is governed by the pore-water composition, temperature, and pressure [N4-F3]. This means that saturation with water is necessary for swelling, but the exact chemistry of the pore water determines whether dissolution or precipitation dominates and whether the reaction proceeds under conditions favorable to gypsum formation [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that the swelling potential is strongly dependent on the specific surface area of the anhydrite crystals, so finely dispersed anhydrite is particularly prone to swelling [N4-F3]. This shows that not all clay-sulfate rocks respond equally; mineralogy and surface area matter [N4-R2][N4-F3].

Hydration and mineral reactions change rock volume through a combination of clay swelling and anhydrite-to-gypsum transformation. The evidence states that the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum results in a volume increase of up to 61% [N4-F3]. In a closed system, the volume of gypsum is about 10% less than that of its reactants, so a net volume increase only occurs if the sulfate mineral expansion is not compensated by a decrease in pore water volume [N1-F1]. In an open system, water inflow is required for swelling to occur because the water uptake by anhydrite to form gypsum must be accompanied by concurrent water inflow [N1-F1]. This means that groundwater is not only a trigger; it is a necessary medium for the swelling reaction to proceed and for the rock to expand [N1-F1][N4-F3].

The most-prone clay-sulfate minerals are anhydrite and gypsum-bearing clay-sulfate rocks, with anhydrite being especially significant because its hydration into gypsum is the main mechanism of swelling [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that expansive clay minerals such as corrensite may play an important, though not clearly defined, role [N4-F3]. In addition, finely dispersed anhydrite crystals are particularly prone to swelling due to their relatively large surface area in potential contact with water [N4-F3]. So the most-prone zones are those with high anhydrite content, high surface area, and favorable pore-water chemistry [N4-F3]. Clay minerals themselves contribute by enabling water access through osmosis and hydration [N3-R3].

## How geochemical conditions control clay-sulfate swelling

Geochemical conditions control clay-sulfate swelling through pore-water chemistry and solubility thresholds. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that the conditions controlling dissolution and precipitation of sulfate minerals depend strongly on the geochemistry of the pore water [N4-R2]. In particular, the mineralogical transformation of anhydrite into gypsum takes place indirectly via the solution phase, with anhydrite dissolving into the pore water and gypsum subsequently precipitating from the solution [N4-F3]. This shows that swelling is not just a mechanical response; it is a geochemical reaction that depends on whether the pore water is undersaturated or oversaturated relative to gypsum [N4-F3].

Pore-water chemistry and solubility thresholds drive expansion by determining whether anhydrite dissolves or gypsum precipitates. The evidence states that dissolution and precipitation equilibria are controlled by pore-water composition, temperature, and pressure [N4-F3]. It also notes that under low-pressure and low-temperature conditions, which are relevant to Gypsum Keuper formations and tunneling, anhydrite solubility is higher than that of gypsum under certain conditions [N4-F3]. This implies that the geochemical threshold is critical: if the pore water promotes anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation, swelling will occur; if not, the reaction will be suppressed or reversed [N4-F3]. The evidence further states that the swelling potential is strongly dependent on the specific surface area of the anhydrite crystals, so finely dispersed anhydrite is particularly prone to swelling [N4-F3]. This means that the same rock type may behave differently depending on its mineralogy and pore-water chemistry [N4-R2][N4-F3].

Dissolution/precipitation reactions alter effective stress because they change the pore-water volume and the hydraulic properties of the rock mass. The evidence explains that changes in pore water volumes can occur by anhydrite solution and gypsum precipitation during the swelling process [N1-F1]. It also states that hydrodynamic conditions are altered by engineering activities and that reaction kinetics depend on the available reactive mineral surfaces and hydrodynamic conditions [N4-F3]. In the excavation context, this means that swelling can feedback into the stress state by changing the rock’s hydraulic properties and effective stress [N4-F3]. The evidence further notes that the hydraulic properties of discontinuities can be altered by gypsum crystallization, which can change local permeability and flow behavior [N4-F3]. Thus, geochemical reactions do not just cause volume expansion; they can also modify the mechanical response of the rock and the surrounding ground [N4-F3].

In addition, the study notes that the geochemical processes affecting the CaSO4−H2O system can be characterized by stability fields of anhydrite and gypsum under various conditions, which can help identify critical conditions leading to sulfate dissolution or precipitation [N4-F3]. Therefore, geochemical indicators are most useful when they can be tied to solubility thresholds and the actual pore-water conditions in the rock [N4-R2][N4-F3].

## Coupled excavation-groundwater-swelling pathway and risks

The coupled excavation-groundwater-swelling pathway is built on a feedback loop in which tunnel excavation changes groundwater flow, which in turn creates conditions favorable for swelling, which then alters the rock mass and can amplify further flow redistribution. This is the key acceleration mechanism: excavation moves water into the rock mass, which then triggers the geochemical reaction that expands the rock [N1-F1][N5-R4].

The feedback loops between water ingress and rock expansion are central. Water entering the rock mass increases saturation and pore-water chemistry, which promotes anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence explains that dissolution and precipitation equilibria are controlled by pore-water composition, temperature, and pressure, and that reaction kinetics depend on available reactive mineral surfaces and hydrodynamic conditions [N4-F3]. In turn, the swelling reaction alters pore-water volume and hydraulic properties, which can change the stress state and effective stress in the rock mass [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The evidence further notes that gypsum crystallization can alter the hydraulic properties of discontinuities, changing local permeability and flow behavior [N4-F3]. So the loop is not just mechanical: water ingress → geochemical reaction → rock expansion → altered stress and permeability → more localized or redirected flow [N1-F1][N4-F3][N6-R1].

The most relevant failure modes in tunneling are tunnel heave, destruction of the tunnel lining, uplift of the entire tunnel and the ground surface above, and the associated engineering disruption and high additional costs [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that swelling problems are especially serious in tunneling because the same mechanisms that cause heave can destroy the tunnel lining and threaten the surface above the tunnel [N1-F1]. In addition, the upstream geochemical evidence indicates that finely dispersed anhydrite crystals are particularly prone to swelling, and that expansive clay minerals such as corrensite may also play an important role [N4-F3]. This means that the failure modes are not just structural; they are also geochemical, and the most vulnerable zones are those where anhydrite is present, permeability has increased, and pore-water chemistry favors gypsum precipitation [N4-F3][N1-F1].

## Overall synthesis

Putting the evidence together, tunnel excavation affects groundwater flow and leads to swelling in clay-sulfate rocks through a three-part mechanism:

1. **Excavation changes groundwater flow and stress** by creating new flow paths, lowering hydraulic heads, and altering permeability through stress relief [N1-R3][N1-F1][N6-R1].
2. **Groundwater interacts with clay-sulfate rocks to induce swelling** through hydration and mineral reactions, especially the hydration of anhydrite into gypsum, which can increase rock volume by up to 61% [N4-F3].
3. **Geochemical conditions control whether the swelling reaction proceeds** by determining pore-water chemistry, solubility thresholds, and the effective stress state [N4-R2][N4-F3].

The result is a coupled feedback pathway: excavation-induced flow change → increased water access and permeability → geochemical reaction (anhydrite dissolution/gypsum precipitation) → rock expansion and swelling → feedback on flow and stress → potential failure modes such as heave, lining damage, and surface uplift [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3][N6-R1]. Tunnel excavation affects groundwater flow and leads to swelling in clay-sulfate rocks through a coupled hydro-mechanical-chemical process. The evidence shows that excavation creates new flow paths and pressure changes by removing the overlying load and allowing water to move into the excavation zone [N1-R3][N1-F1]. At the same time, stress relief from excavation changes permeability and water movement by opening fractures and discontinuities, which can facilitate lateral flow and chemical transformation [N6-R1]. These effects combine to alter the groundwater flow system, change the hydraulic head and pore-pressure field, and modify capture zones and geochemical conditions around the tunnel [N1-R4][N1-F1]. In fractured rock and aquifers, excavation can drastically change groundwater flow paths and discharges, sometimes within a short period, and can alter the aquifer’s budget and create hazards such as mud and water inrush, spring depletion, and ground subsidence [N2-F2]. This establishes the core pathway: excavation-induced disturbance → flow redistribution → stress change → more permeable rock mass.

## How tunnel excavation alters groundwater flow and stress

Excavation creates new flow paths and pressure changes because it disrupts the original subsurface hydraulic system. Groundwater flows into the tunnel during excavation, and the water level falls, causing a decrease in the surface water level [N1-R3]. This means excavation does not simply remove rock; it actively redistributes water and pressure across the surrounding ground [N1-F1]. The hydraulic heads on a slope reflect the steady-state or transient groundwater flow system, and excavation-induced changes can alter those heads [N1-R4]. In practice, tunnel excavation can increase flow rates around the tunnel and change the capture zone of the tunnel and geochemical conditions [N5-R4]. The evidence also notes that tunnel excavation can create pathways for groundwater flow from water-containing units above the tunnel to anhydritic layers at the tunnel invert, which is a key mechanism for redirecting flow into zones where swelling is likely to occur [N1-F1].

Stress relief from excavation affects permeability and water movement by altering the rock mass’s mechanical response. The excavation-damaged zone becomes more permeable as stress is relieved, because fractures and discontinuities can open or become more connected [N6-R1]. This increased permeability allows water to flow laterally, triggering chemical transformation and altering hydrodynamic conditions [N6-R1]. The evidence also states that hydrodynamic conditions are altered by engineering activities on both regional and local scales, which affects solute transport and water accessibility within clay-sulfate rocks [N4-F3]. In the excavation context, this means that stress relief can make the rock mass more vulnerable to water ingress, while the resulting permeability change can either increase or localize flow depending on how the stress field is disturbed [N6-R1][N4-F3].

The zones most vulnerable to flow redistribution are the excavation-damaged zone around the tunnel and the anhydritic layers at the tunnel invert [N1-F1]. The excavation-damaged zone is where the disturbance is most direct, and the tunnel and surrounding rock can act as a conduit for groundwater flow [N1-F1]. The tunnel invert is particularly important because the study explicitly links anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation to water inflow into anhydritic layers, and that process is thought to drive swelling [N1-F1]. These zones are therefore the most exposed to both flow change and subsequent geochemical reaction, making them the most vulnerable to redistribution effects [N1-F1][N4-F3].

## How groundwater interacts with clay-sulfate rocks to induce swelling

Groundwater interacts with clay-sulfate rocks to induce swelling through hydration and mineral reactions that change rock volume. The evidence states that clay-sulfate swelling involves two partially superimposed processes: (1) swelling of clay minerals through osmotic water uptake and hydration, and (2) swelling of sulfates caused by the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum upon contact with water [N4-F3]. This is a key mechanism because it explains how water, not just mechanical stress, can cause expansion [N4-F3].

Water chemistry and saturation levels are important triggers for expansion. The evidence indicates that the conditions controlling dissolution and precipitation of sulfate minerals strongly depend on the geochemistry of the pore water [N4-R2]. In particular, the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum is governed by the pore-water composition, temperature, and pressure [N4-F3]. This means that saturation with water is necessary for swelling, but the exact chemistry of the pore water determines whether dissolution or precipitation dominates and whether the reaction proceeds under conditions favorable to gypsum formation [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that the swelling potential is strongly dependent on the specific surface area of the anhydrite crystals, so finely dispersed anhydrite is particularly prone to swelling [N4-F3]. This shows that not all clay-sulfate rocks respond equally; mineralogy and surface area matter [N4-R2][N4-F3].

Hydration and mineral reactions change rock volume through a combination of clay swelling and anhydrite-to-gypsum transformation. The evidence states that the transformation of anhydrite into gypsum results in a volume increase of up to 61% [N4-F3]. In a closed system, the volume of gypsum is about 10% less than that of its reactants, so a net volume increase only occurs if the sulfate mineral expansion is not compensated by a decrease in pore water volume [N1-F1]. In an open system, water inflow is required for swelling to occur because the water uptake by anhydrite to form gypsum must be accompanied by concurrent water inflow [N1-F1]. This means that groundwater is not only a trigger; it is a necessary medium for the swelling reaction to proceed and for the rock to expand [N1-F1][N4-F3].

The most-prone clay-sulfate minerals are anhydrite and gypsum-bearing clay-sulfate rocks, with anhydrite being especially significant because its hydration into gypsum is the main mechanism of swelling [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that expansive clay minerals such as corrensite may play an important, though not clearly defined, role [N4-F3]. In addition, finely dispersed anhydrite crystals are particularly prone to swelling due to their relatively large surface area in potential contact with water [N4-F3]. So the most-prone zones are those with high anhydrite content, high surface area, and favorable pore-water chemistry [N4-F3]. Clay minerals themselves contribute by enabling water access through osmosis and hydration [N3-R3].

## How geochemical conditions control clay-sulfate swelling

Geochemical conditions control clay-sulfate swelling through pore-water chemistry and solubility thresholds. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that the conditions controlling dissolution and precipitation of sulfate minerals depend strongly on the geochemistry of the pore water [N4-R2]. In particular, the mineralogical transformation of anhydrite into gypsum takes place indirectly via the solution phase, with anhydrite dissolving into the pore water and gypsum subsequently precipitating from the solution [N4-F3]. This shows that swelling is not just a mechanical response; it is a geochemical reaction that depends on whether the pore water is undersaturated or oversaturated relative to gypsum [N4-F3].

Pore-water chemistry and solubility thresholds drive expansion by determining whether anhydrite dissolves or gypsum precipitates. The evidence states that dissolution and precipitation equilibria are controlled by pore-water composition, temperature, and pressure [N4-F3]. It also notes that under low-pressure and low-temperature conditions, which are relevant to Gypsum Keuper formations and tunneling, anhydrite solubility is higher than that of gypsum under certain conditions [N4-F3]. This implies that the geochemical threshold is critical: if the pore water promotes anhydrite dissolution and gypsum precipitation, swelling will occur; if not, the reaction will be suppressed or reversed [N4-F3]. The evidence further states that the swelling potential is strongly dependent on the specific surface area of the anhydrite crystals, so finely dispersed anhydrite is particularly prone to swelling [N4-F3]. This means that the same rock type may behave differently depending on its mineralogy and pore-water chemistry [N4-R2][N4-F3].

Dissolution/precipitation reactions alter effective stress because they change the pore-water volume and the hydraulic properties of the rock mass. The evidence explains that changes in pore water volumes can occur by anhydrite solution and gypsum precipitation during the swelling process [N1-F1]. It also states that hydrodynamic conditions are altered by engineering activities and that reaction kinetics depend on the available reactive mineral surfaces and hydrodynamic conditions [N4-F3]. In the excavation context, this means that swelling can feedback into the stress state by changing the rock’s hydraulic properties and effective stress [N4-F3]. The evidence further notes that the hydraulic properties of discontinuities can be altered by gypsum crystallization, which can change local permeability and flow behavior [N4-F3]. Thus, geochemical reactions do not just cause volume expansion; they can also modify the mechanical response of the rock and the surrounding ground [N4-F3].

Useful geochemical indicators for predicting swelling include pore-water composition, temperature, pressure, anhydrite saturation state, and the presence of expansive clay minerals [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence also implies that the mineralogical transformation of anhydrite into gypsum can be used as an indicator, because the reaction is the main mechanism of swelling in clay-sulfate rocks [N4-F3]. In addition, the study notes that the geochemical processes affecting the CaSO4−H2O system can be characterized by stability fields of anhydrite and gypsum under various conditions, which can help identify critical conditions leading to sulfate dissolution or precipitation [N4-F3]. Therefore, geochemical indicators are most useful when they can be tied to solubility thresholds and the actual pore-water conditions in the rock [N4-R2][N4-F3].
